In terms of lexical stress and vowel distribution, on the other hand, there is not much difference between the three dialects. ... In the Waigeo dialects, if such words have the same vowel in penultimate and final syllables, and end in an open syllable, the final syllable vowel is apocopated when the word appears in sentence-medial context. ... sweep_summary: Kawe (kawe1240) is in the catalog as 'lexical' (contrastive penult/final stress) on Remijsen 2001. this search of works with stress in the title listed exactly one title, Remijsen 2001, which is already held (symlinked into the kawe1240 folder from matb1237) and re-read: sec. 6.2.3 pp. 109-110 states the Waigeo dialects (Kawe, Wauyai, Laganyan) show 'not much difference' from the other Ma'ya dialects in lexical stress, sec. 6.4.3 p. 122 gives the constraints and minimal stress pairs, and App. B.2.6 gives Kawe wordlist forms with stress and phrase-medial apocope; it confirms the classification. Three further sources already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 check (Arnold 2025 Oceanic Linguistics AAM; Arnold 2026 LD&C Wauyai/Batta sketch; Arnold 2024 Zenodo lexical dataset) were read: Arnold 2025 sec. 4.1 gives a Kawe-specific stress minimal pair table (ˈman[a³] vs maˈna³ vs maˈna¹²) from 2023 field data and states stress falls unpredictably on penult or final syllable in all Ma'ya varieties; it also finds lexical tone in Kawe, contra Remijsen's 'atonal' analysis, which refines the catalog record's side-note (the stress coding is unchanged). The Kawe column of Arnold's dataset shows both penultimate (~94) and final (~59) stress on polysyllables by a rough parse, with a few final-stress forms having a non-/a/ penult (meˈtyu³, peˈle¹²y, deˈle³), so Remijsen's vowel-quality constraint is a tendency in Kawe. A Crossref query surfaced Remijsen 2002 (Laboratory Phonology 7, De Gruyter, paywalled), which is chapter 3 of the dissertation on Salawati Ma'ya acoustics, low priority. Best new statement: Arnold 2025 sec. 4.1 / Table 6, proposed as the Kawe-specific deciding source (Remijsen 2001 stays as the co-citation). written at

There is a strong tendency in all varieties for words with penultimate stress to have identical vowels in the penultimate and final syllables: for example, Kawe Ma'ya ˈgulu³m 'rain', ˈbini³ 'hot', taˈbyobo³n 'butterfly' ... In all of the Ma'ya dialects except Misool Ma'ya, if a word has penultimate stress it cannot bear Rise tone ... [Table 6, Kawe:] Penultimate stress: ˈman[a³] 'light (weight)', ˈana 'thing'; Final stress: maˈna³ 'grease', maˈna¹² 'mucus', aˈwat 'root'.

sources.note: Kawe is treated as a dialect of Ma'ya sharing the Ma'ya lexical-stress system: stress is lexically contrastive between penultimate and final syllable (minimal pairs Table VI.7, e.g. 'tala3 'banana' vs ta'la3 'k.o. plant'), partly predictable from vowel quality (non-/a/ penult vowel -> penultimate stress only). Kawe-specific data are the March 2000 Selpale wordlist (App. A.3, B.2.6): penultimate-stressed open-final words apocopate phrase-medially ('tal[a] 'banana', 'tit[i] 'run', 'wun[u] 'swim'); Kawe stated to be atonal (sec. 2.3.1.2.4, 4.4.5). sources.quote: Stress, on the other hand, falls unpredictably on either the penultimate or final syllable of polysyllabic words in all varieties; in at least Salawati Ma'ya, phonetic correlates of stress are increased duration, less centralised vowels, and increased intensity ... There is a strong tendency in all varieties for words with penultimate stress to have identical vowels in the penultimate and final syllables: for example, Kawe Ma'ya ˈgulu³m 'rain', ˈbini³ 'hot', taˈbyobo³n 'butterfly' ... [Table 6, Kawe Ma'ya:] Penultimate stress: ˈman[a³] 'light (weight)', ˈana 'thing'; Final stress: maˈna³ 'grease', maˈna¹² 'mucus', aˈwat 'root'. [fn.12:] Remijsen (2001a: 21, 2001b) analyses Kawe Ma'ya and Wauyai Ma'ya as atonal. Data collected for this project, however, provides evidence for tone in both varieties
sources.locator: sec. 4.1 'Synchrony', AAM pp. 13-14 (the text): Table 4 'Tone in Kawe Ma'ya', Table 6 'Kawe Ma'ya - prosodic patterns in polysyllables', fn. 12
sources.note: Direct 2023 field data on Kawe: lexical stress is unpredictable, penultimate or final, with Kawe minimal/near-minimal pairs ˈman[a³] vs maˈna³ vs maˈna¹²; penultimate-stressed words cannot bear Rise tone; phrase-medial apocope of the final vowel in penultimate-stressed words with identical vowels (as Remijsen). Refines the catalog record's note that Kawe 'has lost lexical tone': Arnold finds High/Rise/toneless contrast in Kawe (Table 4: nu³ 'village' vs nu¹² 'coconut'). Stress coding 'lexical' (contrastive, right-edge two-syllable window) is confirmed.

sources.quote: 283 Kawe forms, transcribed with tone (159 High ³, 105 Rise ¹², 19 toneless) and stress marks; among stress-marked polysyllables my count is 103 penultimate (e.g. ˈtal[a³] 'banana', ˈlapa³k, ˈwamu³ 'breadfruit', meˈriri³n 'cold', taˈbyobo³n) vs 72 final (aˈbo¹²m, afˈni³ 'bat', taˈpu³t, anˈsu³n 'clothes'), none further left. 18 of the 72 final-stressed forms have a non-/a/ penult vowel (giˈni³, deˈle³, peˈle¹²y, teˈtye¹²k, buˈlu³f, teˈmi³, giˈli¹² 'voice'...), so Remijsen's constraint I ('non-/a/ penult => only penultimate stress'), quoted in our prule, does not hold categorically for Kawe.
